source_text: OK that's a good start, but we need another discriminator to separate the R2/R1 R4/R3 R8/R3a cells.  What do you suggest?

fragments.text: but we need another discriminator to separate the R2/R1 R4/R3 R8/R3a cells.

reply_text:
㊥ (separating the three pairs) I'd separate them by what the words are about: the world itself, or your own account of it, meaning a belief, an assumption, the plan or the model. Linguistics has a standard pair of text markers for exactly this. Evidentiality marks where information came from: "I see", "the log shows", "it returned 0.29". That points to the world, giving R2, R4 and R8. Epistemic modality marks how far something is believed: "I think", "I assumed", "so actually", "I was wrong that". That points to the belief, giving R1, R3 and R3a. Unlike Beer and Max-Neef, this reads straight off the words of a turn, so it gives the annotator a concrete test.

🖖 (how it splits each pair)
- **R2 vs R1.** R2 reports what came in: "I ran it and it stalls at step 3". R1 states what is held to be so: "I think the cascade is the bottleneck".
- **R4 vs R3.** Here tense and mood separate as well as the object. R4 is conditional or future, about the world: "if we drop the cap, the queue will flood". R3 changes your mind about how things are or were: "so the 6-hour rule was right after all; I now think…". R4 predicts; R3 revises.
- **R8 vs R3a.** Both are surprise, but at different things. R8 is surprise at the world: "that's odd, it shouldn't have returned anything". R3a is surprise turned on your own belief: "so my assumption about the join key was off".

🖖 (one turn can carry both) A turn like "I looked at the page (R2) and so I now think Kimi misread the spec (R3)" is a perception–belief step happening in one turn. The annotator should be allowed to tag both, in order, without being made to choose. Over time, those sequences are useful evidence about your own loop.

㊟ (why not a philosophical scheme here) I considered Peirce's categories, separating brute encounter from habit or law, and direction of fit. Peirce sorts R2 and R8 well, but puts R4, a law projected forward, on the belief side, which is the wrong cut for us. The evidentiality vs epistemic modality test gets all three pairs right. It's also the kind of thing an annotator can apply consistently, because it rests on wording, not interpretation.

🈸 (go-ahead) If this works for you, I'll add it to the tree as a third split, used only inside the Understanding cells. Then I'll write the tree to a file for the held-out test.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-17
previous_reply_acts.text: (Max-Neef as the discriminator) Here's a draft tree. The first split is Beer's system. Where a system holds more than one R-node, a Max-Neef cell (a need in one of his four modes) separates them, so every leaf is a single R-node. I also fitted the two nodes my last table left out: R5 sits on Beer's System 3–4 balance between present and future, which is the trade-off expected free energy makes, and R10 sits under System 1 as liveness. The Max-Neef terms below are from memory of his matrix in *Human Scale Development* (1991), so they need checking against the source.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-17
previous_reply_acts.text: (where the tree is weakest) Understanding does most of the work twice over: in System 4 and in the model branch, R2/R1, R4/R3 and R8/R3a share cells. Only the Beer branch separates those pairs, by whether the turn is about the world or about what is believed. That may be the right cut. But if the annotator can't tell world-facing from belief-facing, those three pairs will blur. R13 under Protection, as planning to prevent harm, is the placement I'm least sure of.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-17
previous_reply_acts.text: (testing it) The tree would go to the annotator as a short file: Beer's system terms at the first split, then the Max-Neef cell terms at each leaf, with "none" allowed at either level. I'd test it on the half of the 300 sampled turns not used to develop it, against the turn bids, plus about 20 turns for you to judge blind.
